# Source: RELEASE_NOTES.md
URL: https://hela.my.id/library/RELEASE_NOTES.html

# HeLa MCP Ecosystem Release Notes

## v1.11.26 — version records match the code

A housekeeping release. Pins move so that every cell's released commit carries correct
lockfile versions, changelogs and tool documentation. No cell changes its version or
its tools.

## v1.11.25 — the agent asks permission before it acts

Runtime 1.4.5 closes a gap in `hela.agent.run`: a task that said not to modify anything
could still run a model-written shell command, and "do not click Delete" could still
click it. One gate now covers retrieval, planning and dispatch. The same release makes
the default namespaced tool names work and picks the clock for a time question.

Behaviour changes: a ban on any change a shell could make now closes the shell, and
"check that npm test passes" no longer runs the tests. The gate understands English
only. Only the runtime pin changes from 1.11.24.

## v1.11.24 — the agent checks that its answer answers

Runtime 1.4.4 finishes the agent-side contract started in 1.4.2. A run that calls one
tool and gets a non-failing reply is no longer declared complete when that tool has
nothing to do with the task: the loop keeps looking, and says `degraded` if nothing
answers. Smaller fixes keep a permitted copy when the ban only protects the original,
retry a timed-out read once, and make truncated plans and early exits report their
real status. Only the runtime pin changes from 1.11.23.

## v1.11.23 — workflows can reach the other cells

The Mitosis workflow tool existed to chain tools across cells, but out of the box
every step outside Mitosis failed because nothing told the cell where the runtime
was. Runtime 1.4.3 now hands it a private loopback address that only the cell
knows. The same release carries the second pass on the issue author's re-test:
Mitosis planners that finish inside their budget and say precisely what went wrong
with a skill file, an opencode server that agents can actually attach to, memory
tombstones that expire on purpose and cannot be revived by a stale copy, a
`read_graph` page small enough to read, and fact checks and news links that say
what they are. Five cells and the runtime are pinned at their merge commits; the
rest of the snapshot is unchanged from 1.11.22.

## v1.11.22 — a saved browser session loads back as itself

Cytosol 3.3.8 fixes the regression the cookie-scoping change introduced: a
default `browser_save_session` stored `[redacted]` and `browser_load_session`
wrote that text over the live cookie, quietly logging the user out. The session
file is owner-only and scoped to the active page, so it now keeps real values;
redaction applies to what tools return. The same release makes `browser_upload`
refuse credential and system paths even under a broad allowed root, and writes
exports and sessions at mode 0600 atomically. The cytosol pin is the merge
commit of browser-mcp#27; the rest of the snapshot is unchanged from 1.11.21.

## v1.11.21 — the agent stops calling a failure a success

Runtime 1.4.2 closes the agent-side half of the response contract. A tool that
returns `success: false`, `ok: false` or `isError: true` is now a failed call:
the run records it, does not retry the identical call forever, and reports
`status: "failed"` instead of "single action complete". The same commit blocks
a write when the task says not to modify anything, and makes the shared
classifier read `structuredContent` — including `isError` without a `content`
array — so `hela.pipe` cannot fail open on that shape again. Five regressions,
74/74 tests. The runtime is pinned at the merge commit; the rest of the
snapshot is unchanged from 1.11.20.

## v1.11.20 — the doctor counted twice

The host doctor added the runtime's aggregate tool count to the ten cell
counts, then compared that inflated number with the live tool list. On a
bare-name install it warned about hundreds of shadowed tools that did not
exist. It now compares against the cells alone; the only remaining warnings
are real ones. Carries 1.11.17–1.11.19.

## v1.11.19 — the summary matches the check

1.11.18 fixed the permanent "update available" flag but not the summary
printed after an apply, which still listed out-of-profile cells. One-line
follow-up; the install itself was already correct.

## v1.11.18 — the update that stops offering itself

A profile installation was comparing its own cells against the full snapshot,
so a `dev-workspace` host saw `hela-receptor` and `hela-plastid` as newly added
and stayed "update available" forever. The comparison now respects the
installed profile. This release carries 1.11.17 and phenotype 3.3.0.

## v1.11.17 — the whole Ellis design, not a quarter of it

Phenotype 3.3.0 fixes the Ellis UI tools. `get_ellis_ui_template` used to
return `design.md` and `index.html` while that index linked three pages no
tool could fetch; it now returns all four pages, or one when `page` is set.
`list_ellis_ui_designs` drops the 24 repeated design documents for a compact
index, and both tools emit real newlines. The "Zero Dependencies" line in every
template became an accurate description of the Tailwind Play CDN, Google Fonts
and hotlinked icons, with the production caveat.

## v1.11.16 — enzyme tool repair

Enzyme 4.3.3 closes the six-tool roll-up. The headline change is that
`fact_checker` now returns per-source stances and an overall verdict, and
`content_deduplication` returns the surviving objects with what merged into
them instead of a bare list of titles.

## v1.11.15 — synthetic traffic is labelled

Cytosol 3.3.7 tags a request served by a mock rule with the pattern, in the
readable line and structurally, and exposes the active mock count so a session
that forgot to clear them is visible. Closes the last reporting-honesty gap.

## v1.11.14 — one race

Ribosome 3.2.3 stops a bare newline (the Enter key's own echo) from consuming
the pending trigger echo, which flaked the #21 regression under CI. No
behaviour change to the public API.

## v1.11.13 — three roll-ups closed

The remaining Cytosol, Mitosis and Ribosome roll-ups land together. Cytosol
reads structured data instead of guessing, Mitosis prompts point at tools that
exist, and Ribosome stops echoing its own prompt into the session text.

## v1.11.12 — one generator, not two

Phenotype 3.2.2 added its own `docs/TOOLS.md` generator alongside the
ecosystem's, so the two formats overwrote each other and CI failed once the
ecosystem regenerated the file. The local generator is removed; the ecosystem
generator owns the file, and phenotype's consistency test keeps checking README
counts against a live `tools/list`.

## v1.11.11 — tool references caught up

Six cells shipped with a stale `docs/TOOLS.md`: new tools were missing and
descriptions were older than the catalog. The files are regenerated from the
schema catalog and the cells repinned at the docs commits. No behaviour change.

## v1.11.10 — phenotype states only what it can count

Phenotype 3.2.2 replaces hand-written counts with values read from the live
catalogues, deletes two rules the code contradicted, and adds a test that
spawns the server and fails when a published number drifts. Claims that cannot
be derived were removed rather than guessed.

## v1.11.9 — genome writes ask first

Genome 3.2.0 makes the destructive gate consistent: `insert_data`, `update_data`
and `import_data` now need `HELA_GENOME_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE=true`, as `delete_data`
already did. That is a breaking default for bulk writes and is the first line of
the changelog. Also: AWS keys are detected by name, `read_graph` is paged, and a
one-commit repository reports its changes.

## v1.11.8 — boxes say what they measure

Cytosol 3.3.5 returns every vision box twice: normalised `bbox` and `bboxPx`
against the reported image size. A field named `bbox` no longer implies pixels,
which is what made a 48 px element report coordinates up to 971.

## v1.11.7 — one wording fix

Cytosol 3.3.3 rewrote `browser_search`'s description and lost the word
"restricted", which the ecosystem boundary check asserts. The phrase is back and
the cell repinned; behaviour is identical to 3.3.3.

## v1.11.6 — crashes and clocks

Two cells: the browser's new-tab switch crashed on every call and its catalogue
search returned nothing, while genome wrote a fabricated year into harness
timestamps and read `[TAG]` as a date. Both fixed with tests that reproduce the
reported inputs.

## v1.11.5 — derive the tool count, do not retype it

Cytosol gained a tool in 3.3.2, and a hand-written "75 tools" in the site copy
and `llms.txt` failed the docs job. Both the prose and the test now take the
count from the generated catalog.

## v1.11.4 — consent, claims and citations

Three places where a tool acted on the caller's behalf without asking: a
JavaScript `confirm()` was auto-accepted, a mission could be completed by an
agent that did not hold it, and a citation dropped two of three authors. Dialogs
now default to dismiss with an explicit override and a history, missions have
claimant-checked transitions with a lease and an explicit requeue, and citations
follow each style's author rules.

Carries 1.11.3.

## v1.11.3 — Nix hash for the 1.4.1 runtime

The 1.4.1 release changed the package version, which is part of the npm deps
derivation input, so the fixed-output hash stopped matching and the Nix verify
job failed on 1.11.2. The hash is refreshed and the runtime repinned at
`14cc13e`; behaviour is identical to 1.11.2.

## v1.11.2 — a result can now say "degraded"

`hela.pipe` reports `status: ok | degraded | failed` next to `ok`, each step
carries its own status, and a degraded step contributes a reason. A tool that
truncates, filters or substitutes sets that marker; the pipe surfaces it instead
of a clean success. Mitosis 3.1.1 is the first cell to adopt it (`get_skill`).

The nine false-success instances in #8 were already fixed one by one. This
release turns the pattern into a shape that can be tested, documented in the
runtime as `docs/response-contract.md`.

Carries 1.11.1; runtime 1.4.1.

## v1.11.1 — the follow-ups 1.11.0 exposed

Four cells needed a second pass: a deletion that survived project sync but not
central sync, sentiment that still read "never recommend" as praise, tool
payloads sitting in a field MCP clients drop, and React components that ignored
their props. Each fix ships with the test that failed without it.

Carries 1.11.0; runtime unchanged.

## v1.11.0 — six cells that stop guessing

Every fix in this release removes a claim the tool could not support. Trends no
longer call result-page counts "interest". Planners name the tool they will call
or say why they cannot. Analysis tools return `null` instead of a constant.
Cookies are the active page's, redacted. A deleted entity stays deleted. A scan
leaves the database's WAL locks alone, so a write after a scan is not lost.

The rest are failures that were invisible to callers: an orchestrator reporting
failed steps as completed, an agent loop recording `success:false` as `ok:true`,
a `complete` decision with no successful call, dialogs auto-accepted, payloads
dropped because they sat in a non-standard field. Each now says what happened.

Carries 1.10.10; runtime unchanged at 1.4.0.

## v1.10.10 — phenotype measures what it claims

Three of the five fixes in Phenotype 3.1.0 are about claims the tools could not back up.

`design_audit` flagged inline contrast only when the colour strings were identical, so
white-on-white (1.01:1) and yellow-on-white (1.07:1) passed and the page graded A/96. It now
computes WCAG relative luminance; the same page grades B/75 with measured issues. Palette
variants no longer add saturation to greys (an undefined hue was read as red, turning
`#767676` into `#816a6a`), the High Contrast variant names the surface its AAA claim is
measured against, and the derived focus token is clamped into sRGB instead of being emitted
outside it.

The fifth is a surface fix: the five Stitch tools that need the CLI are advertised only when
the CLI resolves — 23 tools instead of 28 on a host without it, with
`HELA_PHENOTYPE_STITCH` to override either way.

Carries 1.10.9; runtime unchanged.

## v1.10.9 — the Nix pin catches up with the runtime fix

Bumping the runtime to 1.4.0 changed the npm-deps derivation input, so `flake.nix`'s
fixed-output hash no longer matched. The runtime repository fixed it; the ecosystem still pinned
the older revision, so the installer and the clean-install CI job kept building the stale tree
and failing at hash verification.

This release pins the corrected revision. Nothing changes at runtime — the runtime code is
identical; only the Nix dependency hash moves.

## v1.10.8 — scoring weights that actually compute

`research_brief` scored candidates without a corpus, so the IDF half of the scorer never
engaged: every term kept a uniform weight and only morphological folding applied. Enzyme
4.2.2 builds the corpus from the pages it returned, so a term present in every title
contributes almost nothing and a rare one carries the match.

Carries 1.10.7; runtime unchanged.

## v1.10.7 — the enzyme fix that actually ships

The backoff and feedback work released as 4.1.0/4.2.0 compiled into
`src/combinedMcp.ts`, while the executable entry (`dist/index.js`) loads the root
`research-server.ts`, which carries its own `research_brief`. Unit tests passed, the pin
said 4.2.0, and the deployed cell still behaved like 4.0.9 — no backoff, no feedback
handle, no spool writes.

Enzyme 4.2.1 ports all three into the entry production runs, and corrects the trigger:
backoff now fires when the **ranked** result is empty, since pages that all fall below the
relevance floor still read as "No results from any source".

Found by verifying the deployed cell end to end after the previous release, not by the test
suite, which exercises the other entry. Carries 1.10.6; runtime unchanged.

## v1.10.6 — pipe stops lying about success

`hela_pipe` exists so intermediate results never pass through the model, which means the
model cannot see a step failing — the runtime is the only thing positioned to notice, and it
did not. A three-step chain with a failed middle step returned `ok: true` and then fed the
error string to the next tool, which produced a plausible keyword analysis of `ENOENT`.

Runtime 1.4.0 makes the pipe fail closed: `ok` reflects every step, `failedStep` names the
first failure, `onError` defaults to `stop` (with `continue` for deliberate best-effort), each
result carries its own `ok`, and `{{prev}}` is unset after a failure instead of carrying the
error onward. The next step's payload is now the parsed result rather than the MCP envelope.

The default change is breaking on purpose — a caller checking `ok` was getting an answer that
was wrong. Cells carry forward from 1.10.5.

## v1.10.5 — membrane answers match what happened

Four tools in the filesystem cell returned a shape that promised more than the code did.
Ranged reads split UTF-8 characters and lost them at every chunk edge; extraction dropped
path-traversal entries silently and called the remainder a success; `watch_file` started a
watcher whose events were discarded on return; `compare_files` measured characters where the
rest of the cell measures bytes.

Membrane 3.0.6 fixes the four: boundary-snapped ranges with `startByte`/`endByte`, extraction
that lists every skipped entry and why, buffered watch events collected by polling (and a
wait for chokidar's initial scan), and bytes plus a separate `characters` field.

Carries 1.10.4. Runtime unchanged at 1.3.7.

## v1.10.4 — the priors loop is closed

The adaptive ranking mechanism had been built and never fed. Enzyme observed which source
produced a result a caller actually used, but could not write the table; genome owned it and
nothing called the writer.

Enzyme 4.2.0 now appends one record per observed follow-up to a spool file, with the display
rank so position bias stays visible. Genome 3.0.7 drains that spool into `source_feedback` on
the next `search_priors` or `search_feedback` call: claimed by rename so two processes cannot
import the same line twice, malformed lines skipped, failed inserts put back for a later pass.

The header still reports `priors: static` until five samples accumulate per class — that is
the system being honest, and now it can stop being honest.

Carries mitosis 3.0.9, nucleus 3.0.7 and enzyme's query/scoring work. Runtime unchanged.

## v1.10.3 — Mitosis can see the organism again

Under `--mode runtime` the cells sit behind one endpoint, so Mitosis's config-based peer
discovery found none of them and `validate_tool_chain` rejected every real tool. It now also
reads the runtime's generated `config/tool-catalog.json`, which already knows each cell's
tools and is revision-validated at build time. Verified against the installed catalog: ten
cells, 299 tools.

Availability is three-state rather than two: a discovered server missing a tool is an error,
a server that was not discovered is a warning ("could not be verified"), and a run with no
catalog produces one warning instead of one error per step. The previous behaviour failed in
the direction that discards correct plans.

Carries the nucleus 3.0.7 and enzyme 4.1.0 fixes from 1.10.2. Runtime unchanged at 1.3.7.

## v1.10.2 — the cells stop reporting quiet failures

Two cell releases, both about a step that failed while looking like it succeeded.

Nucleus 3.0.7 runs local commands from a script file rather than through `sh -c`, so a
`pkill -f` in a compound command no longer matches and kills its own wrapper (then reports
exit 1 with empty output), and `pgrep -f` no longer counts the wrapper as a live process.
Its RTK summariser now refuses a summary below 5% of the source, keeps the original output
and names it, and only treats `Error`/`warning` at line start as log mode.

Enzyme 4.1.0 reshapes a query once when every source returns nothing and says so in the
header, since Google CSE over-constrains on long natural-language questions. Scoring folds
`tool`/`tools`-style variants and weights terms by rarity among the candidates, and each
brief now carries the `query_class`/`source` handle needed to record feedback — with the
exact genome call, including when a follow-up tool opens a URL the brief returned.

Runtime unchanged at 1.3.7.

## v1.10.1 — doctor diagnostics for uninstalled and non-default prefixes

Two lookups produced a report that blamed the host for what was really a path miss. Doctor
now says `not installed` instead of `Not checked`, and when every component is missing it
prints the paths it resolved along with the install-then-diagnose commands. Separately, an
installation made with `--runtime` lives under `<profile>-runtime`, but doctor only checked
`<profile>-individual`; it now scans for sibling `<profile>-*` installations and names the
`--mode` or `--prefix` needed to diagnose each one, in human and JSON output alike.

No cell changes: revisions and versions pin unchanged from 1.10.0.

## v1.10.0 — host-layer doctor and a single MCP entry point

The doctor now covers the layer it previously ignored: the wiring between client
applications and the runtime. `node scripts/doctor.mjs --hosts` (also `npm run doctor:hosts`)
checks the interpreter floor derived from cell `engines`, whether `nodejs` is still marked
manual for apt, the gate file the launcher reads, credential-file modes and key presence,
all six client configs, backup exposure, and a live `initialize`/`tools/list` handshake.
Failures are actionable lines; `--repair` re-installs the pinned node package, re-asserts
the manual mark, and fixes credential-file and backup modes. Exit codes stay 0/1/2.

`scripts/host-entry.sh` is now the canonical client entry point, installed as
`~/.local/bin/hela-runtime-mcp`. It resolves the interpreter at spawn time, refuses to
start below the required major, sources one 0600 credentials file, and logs failures
because MCP hosts swallow child stderr. It is PATH-independent: every external command is
absolute, so it can report a stripped environment instead of dying inside it.

[The reliability contract](docs/reliability.md) documents the resulting chain with eight
diagrams. Sources are Mermaid (`assets/diagrams/*.mmd`) and the rendered SVG next to them;
the library pages embed the SVG because the document renderer carries `markdown-it`
without a Mermaid plugin and escapes raw HTML.

Credential handling also changed: every secret found in client-config backups was copied
into mema-vault before those backups were deleted, so `--hosts` reports a clean backup
surface instead of a permanent warning.

## v1.9.6 — pinned modern web guidance

HeLa Phenotype 3.0.3 now bundles Google's Modern Web Guidance agent skill. The skill, CLI package (`1.0.0`), upstream source commit, and guidance corpus (`2026_11_09-5bcc021b`) are pinned. Profiles that include Phenotype receive the skill through the normal skill-sync workflow; the command-line lookup needs Node.js 22+ and outbound network access.

The new [prebuilt-skills catalog](docs/prebuilt-skills.md) maps every bundled skill to its server and all eight profiles, and documents source pins, synchronization, and update handling. The coordinated v1.9.6 snapshot is immutable; `latest-stable` now resolves to it. v1.9.5 and older snapshots remain unchanged.

## v1.8.0 — dedicated Cytosol image analysis

HeLa Cytosol now accepts a dedicated local image path, HTTP(S) image URL, or base64 image directly through `browser_image_analyze`. The tool returns Mirage VLM scene understanding, OCR, object detection, segmentation, spatial relations, and schema-based decisions without launching a browser page. Image inputs are bounded and protected by workspace, content-type, redirect, and SSRF checks.

## v1.7.0 — Cytosol Mirage visual intelligence

HeLa Cytosol now includes first-class local visual intelligence through Cactus Mirage. The `browser_visual_analyze` tool can describe browser screenshots, detect objects, read text, return segmentation data and relations, and extract values against a schema. The Cactus runtime is managed per Cytosol installation while Mirage model weights remain lazy and are cached on first use.

## v1.6.4 — stable snapshot alias correction

The `latest-stable` snapshot now resolves to the coordinated release pins and
versions published in the 1.6.3 cell/runtime release set.

## v1.6.3 — cross-platform maintenance entrypoints

The installer and maintenance workflow is now Node-first. Use `node setup.mjs`,
`setup.ps1`, or `setup.cmd` for installation and doctor checks; `update.ps1` and
`update.cmd` provide the corresponding Windows update path. The Bash entrypoints
remain compatibility shims.

Profile-scoped build, test, clean, and update operations now run through portable
Node scripts. Runtime Needle discovery also recognizes `needle3.exe` and
`needle.exe` automatically. Native Windows cold-install acceptance is still
tracked separately from this source-level portability work.

## v1.6.2 — Plastid and Receptor dependency refresh

Plastid moves to `aa43877` and Receptor to `1b21cb7`, adopting the lockfile updates that had accumulated on their default branches. Both carried open advisories against `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`; the refreshed locks resolve them, and `npm audit` is clean for Plastid's runtime dependencies while Receptor reports none.

Plastid's manifest also declared `"@modelcontextprotocol/sdk": "latest"`. That is why its lockfile drifted without a reviewable diff; it is now `^1.32.2`. Builds and the existing suites pass — 12 Plastid regressions and 123 Receptor tests — and no cell version changed.

Exposure was limited: the SDK advisories concern HTTP transports, body-size limits, and OAuth flows, while Plastid and Receptor run over stdio. Updating still removes the drift and the noise. Hardware, the Blender bridge, GUI clients, and providers remain separate checks.

## v1.6.1 — switch deployment modes in place

`./setup.sh mode --prefix PATH --mode MODE` converts an existing managed installation to another execution mechanism without a second prefix or a data migration. All five modes are valid targets. Profile, snapshot, workspace, transport, port, and the per-cell `data/` directories carry over; host-mode switches reuse packages already built at the pinned revision with a clean worktree, and Docker modes build or drop their image and `compose.json` accordingly.

The command runs the same verification as a fresh installation and generates a new client fragment instead of editing live client settings. Failed verification restores the previous manifest and writes a pending marker so doctor reports the degraded state. Pending or unmanaged prefixes are refused, HTTP targets require a runtime mode, and re-selecting the current mode is an error.

Enzyme stays at 4.0.0 and the runtime at 1.2.0; every cell pin is unchanged from 1.6.0. Tests cover host-family round-trips, transport guards, pending markers, and Docker switches.

## v1.6.0 — consistent Enzyme search input

Pin Enzyme source `eb98982`. `google_search` now takes `query`, matching every other single text search in the cell. The former `q` argument is removed, so a client that still sends it gets an MCP validation error instead of a silent translation; requests that send both fields are rejected as well. Batch tools keep `queries`, and provider HTTP parameters are unaffected internally.

Both Enzyme entrypoints share one strict schema: the query is trimmed and must be non-empty, `num` is an integer from 1 to 10, and unknown fields are refused before any provider call. Enzyme's contract tests cover discovery, dispatch, rejection of obsolete input, and provider failure for the shipped and modular servers; 32 contract tests and 111 total Enzyme tests pass with a clean TypeScript build and no lint errors. Enzyme moves to 4.0.0 because this is a breaking argument change.

The catalog, generated documentation, and profile counts are rebuilt from the new schema. Counts stay at 24 Enzyme tools, so profile totals do not change. Other cells, the runtime, and every snapshot from v1.0.0 to v1.5.3 are untouched.

## v1.5.3 — canonical relation ordering

Pin Genome source `9ba1d0e`. Relation links now render in one canonical order regardless of database insertion order, preventing relation-order-only conflicts after a lossless repair. All 19 suites / 264 tests pass; the TypeScript build and zero-warning source lint pass. The published 1.5.2 snapshot remains unchanged, as do all other cell/runtime pins and package versions.

## v1.5.2 — replicated vault convergence

Pin Genome source `c32ae94`: replicated notes keep the earliest creation timestamp and latest update timestamp, while incoming observation supersets can retain their order without losing database-only facts. The explicit programmatic repair API archives both originals, respects snapshot/lock checks, and permits rejecting a plan before publication. Normal CLI sync does not choose conflict winners automatically.

Genome's 19 suites / 263 tests and TypeScript build pass, including regressions reproducing the previous timestamp/order loops and validating SQL bindings, JSON rows and tool arguments. Source lint reports zero errors and warnings, covers top-level files and fails on warnings. Package versions remain 3.0.0 for cells and 1.2.0 for runtime; this source snapshot records the exact fixed Genome commit. Other pins and historical snapshots are unchanged. Real vault repair and MCP reconnection require separate, backed-up operational verification; no private vault data is published here.

## v1.5.1 — current documentation and bilingual website

Documentation-only refresh: all ten cells remain **3.0.0**, and runtime remains **1.2.0**. The new source snapshot pins the documentation commits without rewriting v1.0.0–v1.5.0. Plastid and Receptor documentation was merged into their default branches without discarding unrelated dependency updates; the snapshot deliberately pins the documentation-only parents, not those dependency changes.

The EN/ID website now loads generated versions, canonical tool names, and profile metadata. Configuration previews use real repository directories and Codex `mcp_servers` sections. Source guides cover all eight profiles, cold discovery, optional integrations, safe backup/restore, and the limits of current verification. Generated private configurations may contain supplied credentials; committed examples are regenerated with a sanitized environment.

Documentation checks cover 74 regression cases plus local links/anchors and structured metadata; the CLI matrix covers 80 combinations. Browser verification covers 64 visible selections per language and all 16 pages at desktop/mobile widths. These are documentation/UI checks, not new authenticated ACP, provider, Android, or Blender acceptance. Publication does not restart the runtime or change deferred access controls, credentials, databases, or vault conflicts.

## v1.5.0 — on-demand runtime and canonical discovery

Runtime **1.2.0** starts cells only when invoked, shares concurrent startup attempts, and discovers schemas without spawning cells. Revision/build/config-aware caches reject stale entries; legacy/corrupt caches fall back to a validated generated catalog. Unknown calls no longer start unrelated cells. Standalone servers, all eight profiles, and the `dev-workspace` default are preserved.

The canonical inventory drives config generation, doctor/version/profile checks, schema catalogs, and generated documentation counts. Doctor can verify exact runtime discovery with no cell startup via `--runtime`. A new immutable v1.5.0 snapshot pins runtime `9c92dbf`; older versioned snapshots are unchanged.

Verification: **32** runtime regressions on both Linux architectures, **16** all-profile namespace-mode checks, **80** client configurations, four probe regressions, and four inventory regressions. Cold/warm measurements are recorded, not treated as universal benchmarks. See [implementation and verification scope](docs/on-demand-runtime.md). ACP authentication, external client reloads, gateway retirement, vault conflict review, hardware/provider integrations, and deferred security remain separate work.

**Servy rollout verified:** public/local discovery exposes 236 tools without starting any cells; the first safe Nucleus call starts only Nucleus. Deployed doctor, catalog, and revision checks pass. Fresh backups and rollback material are retained, and all 633 existing conflict archive files are unchanged. See the [rollout evidence](docs/on-demand-runtime.md#historical-servy-rollout--runtime-120).

## v1.4.0 — memory safety and runtime verification

The v1.4.0 source snapshot pins the published cell revisions and runtime 1.1.0. Older versioned snapshots are unchanged. `latest-stable.json` tracks this source snapshot, not a guarantee that every optional integration or GUI session has been exercised.

- Genome: 19 suites / 242 tests with clean lockfile dependencies, including WAL-safe backups, isolated restore, vault conflicts, repeated imports, and exclusive mission claims.
- Runtime: 20 isolated fault tests covering hung children, SIGTERM/SIGKILL, actual process exit, one restart, profile/cache boundaries, and shutdown cleanup.
- Nix: real Node 22 package builds on x86_64-linux and native aarch64-linux, using pinned inputs and fixed-output npm dependencies.
- Dependencies: clean-install Zod 4 build fixes in Genome and Enzyme; Enzyme's 79 tests and Phenotype's 74 tests pass.
- Ecosystem: ten isolated standalone MCP handshakes and 80 configuration-generation combinations pass. Codex TOML now uses `mcp_servers` and is accepted by the native parser. These are not authenticated GUI tests.
- Discovery: 290 standalone tools with LLM and model-backed agent features disabled; the same isolated `dev-workspace` runtime exposes 230 tools including `hela.pipe`. Feature-enabled deployments can expose additional Mitosis tools and the optional agent alias; query `tools/list` rather than assuming a static total.

Known limits: Zed/Codex ACP authenticated-session verification remains pending; duplicate ownership warnings do not establish a connection failure. Existing live vault conflicts remain archived for deliberate review. Android/Blender discovery is not hardware integration. Endpoint authentication and credential rotation remain operator work, not changes included in this release.

**Servy deployment verified (2026-11-06):** the rooted ARM Nix package serves the eight-cell `dev-workspace` profile under systemd. Local/public discovery returns 236 live tools, versus 230 in feature-disabled probes; all three Genome mission tools are present. Deployed doctor and strict version/pin checks pass. Existing conflict archives and unrelated client processes were preserved. See [deployment evidence and remaining client/gateway work](docs/deployment-2026-11-06.md).

**All-profile follow-up (2026-11-06):** all eight profiles pass runtime startup/discovery, exact tool/schema parity, and safe read-only routing in both namespacing modes (**16/16** checks). All ten standalone cells plus runtime pass strict version/pin verification; the 80 client-configuration combinations and four probe regressions pass. Machine selections and release snapshots are unchanged. See [profile verification](docs/profile-verification-2026-11-06.md).

## Historical v1.0.0 notes

We are proud to announce the official **v1.0.0** release of the **HeLa MCP Ecosystem** — a modular, immortal cellular AI tooling stack built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), engineered by Azzar.

---

## Architectural Vision & Metaphor

The **HeLa MCP Ecosystem** is named in respectful recognition of **Henrietta Lacks** (1920–1951) and the enduring scientific legacy of HeLa cells. Using a **cellular biology metaphor**, the ecosystem organizes 10 specialized MCP servers into a harmonious organism:

* **Cellular Specialization**: Distinct organelles (Nucleus, Membrane, Enzyme, Ribosome, Plastid) perform targeted domains.
* **Deterministic Immortality**: Environments can be snapshot-pinned (`config/snapshots/v1.0.0.json`) and restored cleanly on any machine.
* **Repository Independence**: Underlying source repositories, technical package names, and Git commit histories remain 100% autonomous.

---

## Key Highlights & Milestones Delivered

### 1. Dual-Backbone Architecture
Every profile is grounded by two core backbones:
* **HeLa Mitosis (`chaining-mcp`)**: Cellular division and orchestration backbone. Bundled Needle 3 agent runtime (plan → execute → observe, offline-first), Needle-backed sequential reasoning (`sequentialthinking`, `agent_run`), task decomposition, and 40 domain prompts. No external sequential-thinking server.
* **HeLa Genome (`Project-Guardian-mcp-server`)**: Living memory and state backbone. SQLite knowledge graph (`memory.db`), entity-relation tracking, cross-session context restoration, and decision memory.

### 2. 10-MCP Component Taxonomy
* **HeLa Membrane** (`filesystem-mcp-server`): Sandboxed workspace filesystem operations and search.
* **HeLa Nucleus** (`terminal-mcp-server`): Isolated command execution with RTK token optimization.
* **HeLa Ribosome** (`menager-mcp-server`): Interactive PTY session multiplexing and Regex hook engine.
* **HeLa Enzyme** (`research-assistant-mcp-server`): Unified Google Custom Search + Wikipedia caching.
* **HeLa Cytosol** (`Browser-Agent`): Playwright browser automation and DOM accessibility perception.
* **HeLa Phenotype** (`the-designer`): UI/UX design tokens, OKLCH palettes, and Tailwind component synthesis.
* **HeLa Receptor** (`scrcpy-mcp`): Android mobile automation via ADB bridge.
* **HeLa Plastid** (`ll3m-agent`): Autonomous Blender procedural 3D modeling and rendering.

### 3. Diagnostic Health Checker (`setup.sh doctor`)
Comprehensive automated diagnostic tool auditing host prerequisites (Node.js >=18, Git, SQLite3), server builds, commit pins, stdio JSON-RPC smoke readiness (<300ms), external runtimes (Playwright, ADB, Blender), and zero-key offline fallback modes.

### 4. 70-Combination Multi-Client Matrix (`npm run test:matrix`)
Full verification across all 10 client backends (Cursor, Claude, Gemini, Antigravity, OpenCode, Kilo, Zed, Codex TOML, Docker Compose, Skip) and 7 agent profiles with 100% schema accuracy.

### 5. Master Integration Test Suite (`npm test`)
Automated stdio JSON-RPC handshake and tools discovery across all 10 servers (**295 active tools discovered and validated in 2.5s**).

### 6. Interactive Documentation Website (`docs/site/`)
Modern, responsive documentation landing site featuring:
* Interactive live Client & Profile Configurator.
* Video showcases & embedded YouTube demos.
* Uploaded Asciinema terminal casts.
* Searchable 10-MCP Cellular Taxonomy directory.

---

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Hela-Ecosystem/hela-mcp-ecosystem.git
cd hela-mcp-ecosystem
./setup.sh doctor
./setup.sh
```

# Source: docs/architecture.md
URL: https://hela.my.id/library/docs/architecture.html

# HeLa MCP Ecosystem Architecture

This document provides a comprehensive architectural reference for the **HeLa MCP Ecosystem**, detailing its cellular design principles, dual-backbone topology, component taxonomies, and cross-MCP communication mechanisms.

Current package versions and feature-dependent tool counts are generated in [current versions](current-versions.md). Each of the ten MCP cells has its own version; the ecosystem snapshot and optional runtime have independent versions.

![Blotcat acting as a conductor in front of a modular system of interconnected server blocks](../assets/blotcat-architecture.jpg)

## Organelle video explainers

Short video introductions to all ten organelles are embedded in the [Architecture reference page](site/architecture.html#organelle-videos). The [complete ecosystem explainer](https://youtu.be/1qv5kD3qApQ) covers their roles and collaboration.

* [Mitosis — Orchestration & Routing](https://youtu.be/SV9HRh5iFWY)
* [Genome — Memory & Context](https://youtu.be/3w39n0Dtuy8)
* [Membrane — Filesystem Access](https://youtu.be/SIO7em0XLA8)
* [Nucleus — Command Execution](https://youtu.be/Msy-_oR_y68)
* [Ribosome — Persistent Workers](https://youtu.be/0pScB7HlMtc)
* [Enzyme — Research & Retrieval](https://youtu.be/fnIy0RzaevM)
* [Cytosol — Browser Automation](https://youtu.be/BvW25O6v-8U)
* [Phenotype — Design Tokens & UI Systems](https://youtu.be/8k6fpEBT3cY)
* [Receptor — Android Device Automation](https://youtu.be/5cy9ZjyLic8)
* [Plastid — Procedural 3D Modeling](https://youtu.be/7TMHqKB2DR8)

---

## 1. Architectural Philosophy: The Cellular Metaphor

The **HeLa MCP Ecosystem** is architected around a cellular biology metaphor, respectfully recognizing **Henrietta Lacks** (1920–1951) and the immortal legacy of HeLa cells in biomedical research:

1. **Cellular Specialization**: In biological systems, organelles perform distinct biochemical functions while cooperating as a unified organism. In the HeLa ecosystem, servers act as specialized cellular components (Nucleus, Membrane, Enzyme, Ribosome, Plastid) coordinated by a dual backbone.
2. **Reproducible source selection**: Commit-pinned snapshots under `config/snapshots/` select known revisions. Platform dependencies and external integrations still require separate validation.
3. **Repository Autonomy**: Underlying repositories, Git histories, and package dependencies remain completely autonomous and uncoupled.

---

## 2. The 4-Tier Naming Architecture

To balance brand clarity, backwards compatibility, and technical provenance, the ecosystem enforces a 4-tier naming model:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T1["Tier 1: Public Identity<br/>HeLa Genome"]
    T2["Tier 2: Machine ID<br/>hela-genome"]
    T3["Tier 3: Technical Repo<br/>project-mcp"]
    T4["Tier 4: Immutable Commit<br/>72bca15ebe..."]

    T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4
```

1. **Tier 1 (Public Identity)**: Clean, uniform human-facing persona name (e.g. *HeLa Mitosis*, *HeLa Genome*, *HeLa Membrane*).
2. **Tier 2 (Machine Identifier)**: Stable hyphenated identifier (`hela-*`) used in configuration files (`mcpServers`), CLI flags, and profile definitions.
3. **Tier 3 (Technical Source Repo)**: Independent Git repository name on GitHub maintaining upstream authorship and commit history.
4. **Tier 4 (Immutable Commit Pin)**: Exact SHA-1 hash recorded in `config/snapshots/` ensuring reproducible builds.

---

## 3. Dual-Backbone Coordination Topology

Every deployed profile in the ecosystem is grounded by a dual backbone:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Client["AI Client / Orchestrator"]

    Mitosis["HeLa Mitosis<br/>(hela-mitosis)<br/>- Dynamic Routing<br/>- Step Reasoning<br/>- Task Decomposition<br/>- Prompt Catalog"]
    Genome["HeLa Genome<br/>(hela-genome)<br/>- Knowledge Graph<br/>- Living SQLite DB<br/>- Entity / Relations<br/>- Milestones & State"]

    Membrane["HeLa Membrane<br/>(Files)"]
    Nucleus["HeLa Nucleus<br/>(Exec)"]
    Ribosome["HeLa Ribosome<br/>(PTY)"]
    Enzyme["HeLa Enzyme<br/>(Search)"]
    Cytosol["HeLa Cytosol<br/>(Browser)"]
    Phenotype["HeLa Phenotype<br/>(Design)"]

    Client -- "stdio JSON-RPC" --> Mitosis & Genome
    Mitosis <-->|"Shared Memory"| Genome
    Mitosis & Genome --> Membrane & Nucleus & Ribosome & Enzyme & Cytosol & Phenotype
```

* **HeLa Mitosis (Routing & Planning Backbone)**: Bundled Needle 3 agent runtime (plan → execute → observe with recorded AgentState), suggests multi-step execution paths, Needle-backed sequential analysis, and serves 40 curated domain prompts. Offline-first; OpenRouter is an escalation backend only.
* **HeLa Genome (State & Memory Backbone)**: Maintains the living SQLite knowledge graph (`memory.db`), restores cross-session context, records task states, and manages project milestones.

---

## 4. Component Taxonomy

### 4.1 Core Backbone Servers

#### 1. HeLa Mitosis (`hela-mitosis` / `chaining-mcp`)
* **Role**: Orchestration, dynamic routing, and Needle-backed sequential reasoning.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/index.js`
* **Tools**: `agent_run`, `sequentialthinking`, `analyze_with_sequential_thinking`, `analyze_tools`, `generate_route_suggestions`, `llm_decompose_task`, `llm_suggest_route`, `workflow_orchestrator`, `workflow_status`, `workflow_cancel`, `list_skills`, `search_skills`, `get_skill`, `suggest_skill_chain`, plus prompt/resource, time, and validation tools.
* **Zero-Key Behavior**: The bundled Needle 3 agent runs fully offline. Without `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, escalation hands control back to the calling agent (`handoff: true`) with the full state trail — never a fabricated answer. `brainstorming` is the one exception: it needs a generative model and fails honestly without a key.

#### 2. HeLa Genome (`hela-genome` / `project-mcp`)
* **Role**: Living memory graph, entity-relation-observation state tracking.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/index.js`
* **Tools**: `memory_edit` (entity/relation/observation CRUD), `read_graph`, `search_nodes`, `get_session_context`, `sync_central_memory`, `security_scan`, and the three mission tools `create_mission`, `list_missions`, `update_mission`.
* **Storage**: Embedded SQLite database (`memory.db`) with FTS5 full-text indexing.

---

### 4.2 Core Capability Servers

#### 3. HeLa Membrane (`hela-membrane` / `filesystem-mcp`)
* **Role**: Sandboxed workspace filesystem operations and search.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/index.js`
* **Tools**: `read_file`, `write_file`, `find_files`, `search_in_files`, `copy_file`, `move_file`, `delete_file`, `archive_files`.

#### 4. HeLa Nucleus (`hela-nucleus` / `terminal-mcp`)
* **Role**: Isolated command execution and RTK token optimization.
* **Entrypoint**: `build/index.js`
* **Tools**: `execute_command`, `transfer_file`, `terminal_ls`, `terminal_grep`, `terminal_cat`, `terminal_session_close`, `terminal_session_list`.

#### 5. HeLa Ribosome (`hela-ribosome` / `menager-mcp`)
* **Role**: Polyglot interactive PTY session multiplexing and Regex hook engine.
* **Entrypoint**: `build/index.js`
* **Tools**: `session_spawn`, `session_write`, `session_read`, `session_hook`, `session_close`, `session_list`, `session_prune`.

#### 6. HeLa Enzyme (`hela-enzyme` / `researcher-mcp`)
* **Role**: Unified research platform: zero-key dual-tier web search + arXiv + Google News RSS + Wikipedia caching.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/index.js`
* **Tools**: `google_search`, `wikipedia_search`, `wikipedia_get`, `content_summarizer`, `fact_checker`, `keyword_extraction`.

#### 7. HeLa Cytosol (`hela-cytosol` / `browser-mcp`)
* **Role**: Playwright-based browser automation with accessibility and DOM perception, screenshot verification, OCR, and dedicated image analysis through the local Mirage VLM. It can analyze a standalone image without launching a browser page.
* **Entrypoint**: `src/server.js`
* **Tools**: `browser_navigate`, `browser_screenshot`, `browser_click`, `browser_type`, `browser_get_content`, `browser_visual_analyze`, `browser_image_analyze`, `browser_ocr`, and `browser_extract_schema`.

---

### 4.3 Specialized Capability Servers

#### 8. HeLa Phenotype (`hela-phenotype` / `designer-mcp`)
* **Role**: UI/UX design tokens, OKLCH palettes, and Tailwind component synthesis.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/index.js`
* **Tools**: `design_tokens`, `palette`, `design_audit`, `generate_template`, `logo_workflow`.

#### 9. HeLa Receptor (`hela-receptor` / `scrcpy-mcp`)
* **Role**: Android mobile device control via ADB bridge.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/server.js`
* **Tools**: `start_session`, `ui_dump`, `ui_find_element`, `tap`, `swipe`, `input_text`, `screenshot`.

#### 10. HeLa Plastid (`hela-plastid` / `ll3m-mcp`)
* **Role**: Autonomous 3D procedural modeling and rendering in Blender.
* **Entrypoint**: `dist/index.js` (under `brain/`)
* **Tools**: `generate_modeling_plan`, `execute_blender_code`, `render_output`, `save_blend`, `get_fast_feedback`.

---

### 4.4 Canonical Tool Boundaries (v1.2.1)

Several organelles expose overlapping capabilities. Descriptions and the Mitosis capability router now enforce a single canonical choice per intent, keeping a restricted alternative only for its niche:

| Intent | Canonical | Restricted alternative | Restricted use |
|--------|-----------|------------------------|----------------|
| Web search | `hela-enzyme:google_search` | `hela-cytosol:browser_search` | Visual browser workflows only |
| Content extraction | `hela-enzyme:extract_content` | `hela-cytosol:browser_get_content` | Pages requiring client-side JavaScript |
| Local file read | `hela-membrane:read_file` | `hela-nucleus:terminal_cat` | Remote SSH targets only (`host` required) |
| Memory-graph inspection | `hela-genome:execute_sql` / `query_data` | `hela-ribosome:opencode_db` | OpenCode session database only |

Tool names are unique ecosystem-wide after the Phase 1 rename, so the router matches boundaries by tool name without needing a server field.

---

### 4.5 HeLa Runtime (optional daemon, `hela-runtime`)

The optional runtime supervises child MCP processes behind one stdio or Streamable HTTP endpoint. Its generated catalog exposes selected-profile schemas without starting cells. The first invocation starts only its target; concurrent first calls share startup. Unknown tool names do not trigger an all-cell scan.

- **Source:** https://github.com/Hela-Ecosystem/hela-runtime
- **Entry:** `hela-runtime/dist/index.js`
- **Serve mode:** add `--runtime` to any profile, for example `node setup.mjs --profile dev-workspace --client opencode --runtime`. Runtime is not a profile; an omitted profile defaults to `minimal`.
- **Env:** `HELA_ECOSYSTEM_ROOT`, `HELA_PROFILE`, `HELA_HTTP_PORT`, and `HELA_NAMESPACE_TOOLS` — namespacing is on by default, and `HELA_NAMESPACE_TOOLS=0` restores bare cell-local tool names for clients that pin them.
- **Features:** true on-demand ignition for every selected cell, fingerprinted schema caches, bounded crash/timeout recovery, namespacing on by default (a bare `read_file` cannot shadow the host's), runtime-internal `hela.pipe`, and HTTP `/healthz` liveness.
- **Without it:** users keep the individual servers selected by their profile and can use `hela-mitosis:workflow_orchestrator` for cross-cell chaining.
- **Details:** [on-demand startup, cache invalidation and deployment evidence](on-demand-runtime.md).

#### Response contract: ok, degraded, failed

A tool result has three states, and the state is part of the shape. `hela.pipe` returns `status: "ok" | "degraded" | "failed"`, each step carries its own `status`, and a degraded step contributes a reason to a top-level `degraded` array. `ok` stays true for a degraded result; `isError` is reserved for failures. A cell marks degradation with `degraded`, `partial`, `truncated`, `status: "degraded"` or `warnings` on its JSON payload — the object form is preferred because the contract requires a reason. Three rules follow: an assertion needs evidence, a failed payload is never piped onward as input, and degradation must be visible in the shape rather than only in prose. The full contract is in the runtime repository, `docs/response-contract.md`.

## 5. Security & Isolation Model

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Host["Host Operating System / Terminal Environment"]
    Root["HeLa MCP Ecosystem Root"]
    Sandbox["stdio JSON-RPC Sandbox"]
    Membrane2["Path Canonicalization<br/>(HeLa Membrane)"]
    Nucleus2["Explicit CWD & Timeout Limits<br/>(HeLa Nucleus)"]
    Ribosome2["Process Group Teardown<br/>(HeLa Ribosome)"]
    Cytosol2["SSRF IP Filtering<br/>(HeLa Cytosol)"]

    Host --> Root
    Root --> Sandbox & Membrane2 & Nucleus2 & Ribosome2 & Cytosol2
```

1. **Process Boundary**: Each server runs in an isolated Node.js child process communicating exclusively over standard input/output (`stdio`) via JSON-RPC 2.0 messages.
2. **Memory Safety**: SQLite database operations in `hela-genome` use parameterized queries with WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode.
3. **Credential handling**: Doctor reports presence, not values. Generated client configurations can contain explicitly configured credentials; treat those files and generator output as private. Process separation is not a security sandbox, and remote endpoint authentication/authorization remain explicitly deferred; see [security status](security-audit.md).

---

## 6. Profile System & Lifecycle Management

The ecosystem configuration generator (`scripts/generate-config.mjs`) reads:
1. **`config/inventory.json`**: Authoritative component catalog, entrypoints, Git repositories, and alias mappings.
2. **`config/profiles.json`**: Curated stacks tailored to specific agent personas and hardware targets.

The installer matches the selected profile against the inventory and chosen snapshot, then renders client syntax: `mcpServers` JSON, OpenCode/Kilo `mcp`, Zed `context_servers`, or Codex `[mcp_servers.*]` TOML. Runtime installation also refreshes selected-profile schema catalogs. All eight profiles are supported; lappy's full ten-cell roster and servy's eight-cell roster are installation choices, not code forks.

# Source: docs/beginner-guide.md
URL: https://hela.my.id/library/docs/beginner-guide.html

# Beginner's Guide: HeLa MCP Ecosystem

![Blotcat beginner setup](../assets/blotcat-beginner.jpg)

HeLa connects an AI client to tools for memory, files, commands, research, design, browsers, Android, and Blender. Install only the profile you need. Tools can change files and run commands with the server account's privileges; review your client's permissions before use.

Current software versions are listed in [current versions](current-versions.md). Setup time depends on dependencies and downloads; browser and hardware workflows need extra software.

## Requirements

- Node.js **22 LTS** is the tested full-stack environment. Enzyme requires at least 20.18.1; Receptor requires 22. Individual packages can declare different standalone engine ranges.
- Git and a terminal. Use Node directly on Linux/macOS, or `setup.ps1` in Windows PowerShell / `setup.cmd` in Command Prompt. `setup.sh` remains available as a Unix compatibility shim.
- Optional capabilities: Chromium/Playwright for browser work; the local Mirage model for Cytosol visual analysis, OCR, detection, segmentation, and standalone-image inspection; ADB and a device for Android; and the Blender bridge for 3D.

Needle and Mirage are profile capabilities rather than separate client deployments. Needle is installed with every canonical profile through Mitosis. Mirage is installed only by profiles that include Cytosol: `dev-workspace`, `research`, `web-devops`, and `all`. Selecting one of those profiles installs both automatically; selecting `minimal`, `headless-server`, `android-testing`, or `3d-modeling` does not install Mirage.

## Install a profile

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Hela-Ecosystem/hela-mcp-ecosystem.git
cd hela-mcp-ecosystem
node setup.mjs --mode runtime --profile dev-workspace --client opencode --non-interactive
```

On Windows PowerShell, run `.\setup.ps1 --mode runtime --profile dev-workspace --client opencode --non-interactive`; in Command Prompt, use `setup.cmd` with the same arguments. Change the client to `cursor`, `claude`, `gemini`, `antigravity`, `kilo`, `zed`, or `codex` as appropriate. The installer prints its managed prefix and a private client fragment: review and merge that fragment into your client settings. It does not overwrite existing client files or reuse your working repositories. Run `node setup.mjs` without flags for interactive profile/mode/client selection.

All eight profiles are supported:

- `minimal`: three research/memory cells.
- `dev-workspace`: eight development/browser/design cells; select it explicitly when you need the broader workstation stack.
- `headless-server`: seven cells without browser/device dependencies.
- `research`: five research/browser/workspace cells.
- `web-devops`: six frontend/browser/design cells.
- `android-testing`: five cells including device control.
- `3d-modeling`: five cells including Blender.
- `all`: all ten cells.

See [profiles](profiles.md) for membership. Your selection is independent of other machines: lappy's ten-cell roster and servy's eight-cell roster are examples, not required configurations for everyone.

## One connection or separate servers

The installer normally configures separate MCP servers. Add `--runtime` to keep the same profile behind one endpoint:

```bash
node setup.mjs --profile dev-workspace --client opencode --runtime --non-interactive
```

Runtime is a serve mode, not a profile named `runtime`. Its catalog advertises schemas without starting cells; a first call starts only its target. [Runtime details](on-demand-runtime.md) explain catalog generation, missing metadata, and recovery.

Other mechanisms are `--mode docker` (separate containers), `--mode docker-runtime` (one runtime container), and `--mode nix` (pinned toolchain and packaged runtime). Runtime modes also support `--transport http`. See [installation modes](installation.md) for exact requirements and commands; Docker needs a working daemon, and HTTP listeners are started explicitly.

## Optional keys

OpenRouter, GitHub, and Google keys are optional for discovery and keyless capabilities. Keyless does **not** mean every operation is offline: web research and external design services still need network access, and generative-model features require their configured provider or local engine. See [keys and services](keys-and-secrets.md).

Generated configuration can contain credentials you explicitly provide. Keep it private, and do not paste the complete file into a chat or issue.

## Verify the selected installation

```bash
node setup.mjs doctor --mode runtime --profile dev-workspace
npm run test:matrix
```

Doctor checks selected paths, versions, revisions, and actual isolated MCP replies. Runtime checking also verifies catalog parity and zero discovery startups. The configuration matrix checks 80 profile/client combinations; it does not log in to GUI agents or exercise hardware.

For an explicit prefix, use `node setup.mjs doctor --prefix /path/to/prefix`. For Docker or Nix defaults, select the same `--mode` and profile as installation. `doctor --url http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp` checks a running HTTP endpoint; it does not inspect remote source revisions.

On a full ten-cell checkout you can also run `npm test` and `npm run test:profiles`. On a partial checkout use `npm run test:profiles -- --profile <id>`. Missing unselected hardware repositories are not a reason to change your machine's profile.

Reload the relevant client deliberately after reviewing configuration changes. Some clients, including Zed, can auto-reload servers when settings are saved. Do not change live vault hooks or restart unrelated clients merely to silence a warning. See [integration](integration.md) and [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

# Source: docs/code-mode-research.md
URL: https://hela.my.id/library/docs/code-mode-research.html

# Code Mode for HeLa: research and design

Status: research. Nothing here is implemented.

The question: should the ecosystem expose **one code-execution tool** instead of (or beside)
hundreds of MCP tool schemas — and what would that cost in security and complexity?

Two independent labs published the same pattern within six weeks of each other, from very
different platforms. That coincidence is the strongest signal in this document. The evidence
is thinner than the blog posts suggest, and the sandbox is the whole problem.

## 1. What Code Mode is

The model receives one tool whose input is source code. That code calls typed functions
representing the connected tools, runs in a sandbox, and returns only its final output.
Intermediate results never enter the model's context.

```
direct tool calling                    code mode
─────────────────                      ─────────
model → tool call → result             model → code ──┐
model → tool call → result                          ├─ sandbox: call, filter, loop
model → tool call → result                          ├─ sandbox: call, join
model → answer                                      └─ return only the answer
```

Three claims are made, and they fail or succeed independently:

1. **Context economy** — schemas and intermediate results stop competing with the task.
2. **Composition** — loops, branches, joins and retries move out of the message loop.
3. **Accuracy** — models write better code than tool-call JSON, because they have seen more
   of it.

Claim 3 is repeated most and evidenced least.

## 2. Evidence, and what each source actually shows

| Source | Claim | What it demonstrates | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anthropic, *Code execution with MCP* (Nov 2025) | 150k → 2k tokens, "98.7%" | One worked example with a generated tool-file tree; illustrative, not a benchmark. Their platform docs separately claim 35–75% input-token reductions on multi-step workflows — the more defensible number | Direction yes, magnitude no |
| Cloudflare, *Code Mode* (Sep 2025) | "Striking" results; more and more complex tools as TypeScript | Qualitative engineering report; no published eval or failure rates | Medium |
| CodeAct (ICML 2024) | Code actions beat JSON/text "up to 20%" | 17 LLMs, API-Bank plus a new benchmark | High for code-as-action; not MCP-specific |

None of them quantify: how often generated code is wrong where a tool call would have
succeeded, what the sandbox costs to operate, or who reviews code that mutates state.

## 3. What it would cost *here*, measured

Measured against this installation's live catalog, not a hypothetical:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Reachable tools in one session | 305 |
| `tools/list` schema size | **161 KB** |
| Estimated tokens (bytes ÷ 4) | **≈ 40,000** |
| Average schema per tool | 528 B |
| Largest single schema | 4.9 KB (`logo_workflow`) |
| Declared across all cells | 591 (286 shadowed by bare-name collisions) |

40k tokens is roughly a fifth of a 200k window, paid before the first request. Namespacing
every tool would make the number worse, not better — 591 schemas. That is the real
motivation: not that code mode is fashionable, but that this catalog is too large to inline.

Two honest caveats:

- Providers cache tool definitions (Anthropic prompt caching, OpenAI automatic caching), so
  the *marginal* cost is lower than 40k per turn. The context window is still occupied, and
  cache reads are cheap but not free.
- The saving only converts to wall-clock or accuracy if the model actually needed most of
  those schemas. For a single-tool task, inlining 305 tools versus loading one costs the same
  either way — and code mode adds a sandbox and a failure mode for nothing.

## 4. Critiques worth taking seriously

- **You still need the types.** Code that calls `membrane.read_file(path, encoding)` must
  know the signature. Without `describe`, models hallucinate parameters; with it, you have
  traded a schema block for a discovery round-trip. Neither is free.
- **Debugging moves to the model.** A failed tool call returns a tool error. Failed code
  returns a stack trace through a sandbox; the retry burns tokens on the whole program, not
  one call.
- **Reviewability drops by default.** Tool calls are individually visible in a transcript;
  one execution that makes forty calls is not, unless the runtime logs each proxied call.
  Auditability must be designed in, not inherited.
- **Prompt injection becomes code execution.** If any tool output can steer the model, the
  blast radius is now "whatever the sandbox allows" instead of "whatever the next tool call
  allows". This is the argument for keeping credentials and network out of the sandbox.
- **It rewards strong models.** CodeAct shows gains across 17 models, but the spread is wide;
  a weaker model writing a 40-line program that half-works is worse than three tool calls.
- **Sandbox dependencies rot.** Native modules (`isolated-vm`) must be rebuilt per Node ABI;
  WASM runtimes are stable but slow. The cheapest robust option is an OS-level boundary
  around a plain Node child process.

## 5. Three designs

**A. Execute + discover inside the runtime (recommended).** Two new tools beside the existing
ones: `hela.execute({code})` and a discovery path (`search`, `describe`). Every sandbox call
proxies back to the runtime, which applies the same roots policy, approvals and audit as a
direct call.

![Code mode flow](../assets/diagrams/09-code-mode-flow.svg)

*Source: [09-code-mode-flow.mmd](../assets/diagrams/09-code-mode-flow.mmd).*

**B. Filesystem of tools.** Generate `servers/<cell>/<tool>.ts` plus `index.ts` and let the
agent read what it needs. Anthropic's shape. Cheapest to bolt on, but it needs a readable
filesystem inside the sandbox and costs more tokens per discovery than one `describe` call.

**C. Keep direct calls.** Correct for small catalogs; at 305 tools it is what we do now.

A and B compose: A's `describe` can serve the same generated text B writes to disk.

## 6. Trust boundary

![Code mode boundary](../assets/diagrams/10-code-mode-boundary.svg)

*Source: [10-code-mode-boundary.mmd](../assets/diagrams/10-code-mode-boundary.mmd).*

The rule that makes the design coherent: **capabilities live in the parent; the sandbox holds
none.** No network, no host filesystem beyond a per-execution workspace, no environment, no
credentials. Tool calls cross one RPC channel that the parent validates. If the sandbox is
compromised, an attacker gets a workspace and a list of tool calls that policy already allows.

## 7. Sandbox options on Linux

| Option | Isolation | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node:vm` in-process | **none** — documented as not a security boundary | <1 ms | Only for trusted snippets; never for model output |
| Node permission model | fs/net/child-process gating | ~25 ms | Useful hardening; still not a security boundary |
| Bun | none by default | low | Reject |
| Deno subprocess | capability-based, deny by default | 30–50 ms | Strong ergonomics; ships a second runtime |
| QuickJS (WASM) | near-perfect (software fault isolation); a guest loop or OOM cannot kill the host | 1–3 ms, slow compute | Excellent fast path for pure data work; async is limited to one concurrent bridge call |
| `isolated-vm` | V8 isolate, memory-isolated | 2–5 ms; native build per ABI | **Avoid**: maintenance mode, fragile C++, a V8 panic takes the host process down with it |
| Child process + `bwrap`/seccomp/Landlock | kernel-enforced namespaces, fs and net | 10–25 ms | Strongest for orchestration; Linux-only |

A two-tier split is possible — route pure data work to an in-process QuickJS isolate, and
only orchestration to a process sandbox. It buys ~20 ms on the cheap path and doubles the
execution surface to maintain. Phase 1 should ship **one** tier; add the fast path only if
measurement shows the process start dominates real tasks.

Recommendation: **child process + `bwrap`/Landlock profile + stdio RPC**, with the
parent enforcing time, memory, call budget and output size. It is not containment against a
kernel exploit; it is containment against `rm -rf ~`, `curl | sh`, and runaway loops — which
is the realistic threat for a local, single-user agent.

Three details that are cheap and easy to forget: mark inherited file descriptors
`O_CLOEXEC` and `close_range(3, ~0)` before exec (a leaked socket is a channel); run with
`--unshare-net`, `--cap-drop ALL`, read-only `/usr` and `tmpfs` `/tmp`; and cap tool calls
per execution (30–50) so an infinite loop cannot hammer an external API even while inside
the time limit.

Note what this machine already grants: the nucleus cell runs arbitrary shell commands today.
Code mode does not add a capability class here; it adds a *narrower, audited* interface and a
place to enforce limits that raw shell access does not have. A sandbox weaker than the
existing shell would be theatre.

## 8. Progressive discovery

Loading 305 signatures up front recreates the problem. Two tools instead:

- `search(query, {limit})` → ranked `{path, cell, tool, one_line}`, no schemas.
- `describe(path)` → one TypeScript signature plus its doc comment.

Both are generated from the same source: a `tools.d.ts` built at boot from each cell's
`tools/list` schema. The file is the catalog's single representation — `search` indexes it,
`describe` serves a slice, and the sandbox can be handed the declarations it asked for.

Detail levels (name / signature / full) matter: triage does not need parameter docs.
Names must be unique for paths to exist, which is the concrete argument for turning
namespacing on: 286 declared tools have no addressable identity today because a later cell
shadows the bare name.

## 9. Execution contract

```
hela.execute({ code, timeout_ms?, max_calls? })
  → { status: "ok" | "error" | "timeout" | "denied",
      result, logs,
      calls: [{ path, ms, ok }],
      duration_ms }
```

Enforced by the parent, not the sandbox: wall clock (default 30 s), output (256 KB, then
truncate with a marker), call count (default 50), memory (rlimit/cgroup).

Failures are data. Sandbox error, tool error and policy denial all return a structured
`status` so the model can retry or report, and the host never dies from generated code.

## 10. Security model

| Threat | Mitigation | Residual |
|---|---|---|
| Injected code exfiltrates files | no network, workspace-only fs, roots policy per call | data can be written into an allowed root and read later |
| Destructive calls (`delete_file`, archive extract) | per-tool approval; mutating tools denied by default in code mode | approved code can still be wrong |
| Resource exhaustion | time, call budget, memory, output caps | legal-but-heavy work still costs CPU |
| Secrets reachable from code | credentials stay in the parent; bindings, not env | a tool returning secrets leaks them into `logs` |
| No audit trail | every RPC logged: path, args digest, duration, execution id | logs hold digests, not payloads |

Approval fatigue is the realistic failure: a prompt people click through is not a control.
Read-only tools should run unprompted; only mutations should stop.

## 11. Implementation plan

Phase 1 — read-only, no approvals:
1. `code-mode/catalog.mjs`: unique path per tool from live `tools/list`; one-line summary and
   full signature per tool.
2. `code-mode/search.mjs`: token-overlap or BM25 over name + description. No embeddings.
3. `code-mode/executor.mjs`: child process, stdio RPC, `bwrap` profile (`--unshare-net`,
   `--cap-drop ALL`, `--tmpfs /tmp`, read-only system paths), `close_range` before exec,
   kill on timeout.
4. Register `hela.execute` and `hela.describe` behind `HELA_CODE_MODE=1`.
5. Tests: escape attempts (fs outside workspace, `fetch`, `process`, infinite loop, memory
   bomb) and golden multi-step tasks.

Phase 2: approval policy for mutating tools; append-only audit log; `--dry-run` returning
planned calls without executing them.

Phase 3: snippets — save a successful execution as a skill under
`~/.local/share/hela/snippets` with a `SKILL.md`, discoverable by `search`. This is the part
that compounds: capability grows without schemas growing.

Measure before/after on three fixed tasks: schema bytes in context, model-mediated calls,
wall time, wrong-tool rate. If the schema saving does not show up as wall-time or error-rate
improvement, stop at phase 1.

## 12. What would make this not worth doing

- If client-side caching keeps schemas out of context, claim 1 mostly evaporates and only
  composition remains.
- If HeLa's task mix is mostly single-tool, code mode adds a sandbox for nothing. Measure the
  mix first.
- If the sandbox ends up in-process, the honest description is "no sandbox", and approvals
  stop being optional.

## Sources

- Cloudflare, *Code Mode: the better way to use MCP* — https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-mode/
- Cloudflare, *Code Mode* and *How Code Mode works* — https://developers.cloudflare.com/agents/tools/codemode/
- Anthropic, *Code execution with MCP* — https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp
- Anthropic platform docs, *Advanced tool use* (search tools, programmatic tool calling) — https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/tool-use
- Wang et al., *Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents* (CodeAct, ICML 2024) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030

# Source: docs/deployment-2026-11-06.md

# Servy deployment verification — 2026-11-06

This records the earlier runtime 1.1.0 rollout. The subsequent [runtime 1.2.0 on-demand deployment](on-demand-runtime.md#historical-servy-rollout--runtime-120) supersedes its process/startup state; the evidence below remains historical.

The v1.4.0 source release (`c9faa9b`) is deployed to servy's systemd-managed HTTP runtime. This record covers that deployment, not authenticated GUI sessions or live vault reconciliation.

## Published source and builds

- Genome: `16fc4f31735e139d690ae0ace8d4feaf1a603563`.
- Enzyme: `5399e33c7c8a5b75ad620dc33f66a1cbf49972f7`.
- Runtime: `797bad451b45d0d67631eeb8cdb1c93d259f614c`, version **1.1.0**.

# Servy runtime update — 2026-11-19

Records the lappy → servy rollout of ecosystem **1.9.19** and runtime **1.3.3**. Evidence for this host only; it does not describe other machines.

## Host layout (unchanged by this update)

- Source checkouts: `/home/ubuntu/MCPservers/*` (ecosystem, runtime, eight cells).
- Service: `hela-runtime.service`, `HELA_PROFILE=dev-workspace`, `HELA_ECOSYSTEM_ROOT=/home/ubuntu/MCPservers/hela-mcp-ecosystem`, HTTP on `0.0.0.0:8090`.
- Roster: **eight cells** — Mitosis, Genome, Membrane, Nucleus, Ribosome, Enzyme, Phenotype, Cytosol. Receptor and Plastid are deliberately absent: this host has neither `adb` nor `blender`. Lappy runs the ten-cell `all` roster; the difference is an installation choice, not a code fork.
- ExecStart comes from the `10-nix-package.conf` drop-in and points at a wrapper in a dated deployment directory, which execs a Nix-built runtime with the pinned Node 22.23.4.

## What ran

1. `memory.db`, `hela-runs.db` and the local tool-catalog copy backed up to `/home/ubuntu/.local/state/hela/backups/pre-1.9.18-20261119T015844Z/`.
2. All ten checkouts pulled fast-forward to the 1.9.19 revisions (`hela-runtime` 6ca8b61, ecosystem 61f848e, cells at their release commits). `researcher-mcp` was on a detached HEAD and was moved onto `master` first.
3. Cells rebuilt (`npm ci` + `npm run build`) — eight cells plus runtime, all green.
4. Runtime packaged with Nix: `hela-runtime-1.3.3` at `/nix/store/pc49i4nc1qs7nfkkk5mz81mnc9jqj508-hela-runtime-1.3.3`, GC-rooted at `~/.local/state/hela/gcroots/runtime-1.3.3`.
5. Staged wrapper under `~/.local/state/hela/deployments/servy-1.9.18-20261118T190500Z/`, smoke-tested on port 8091 (health reported 1.3.3) before touching the live unit.
6. Drop-in backed up, ExecStart switched, `daemon-reload`, `systemctl restart`. Old deployment directory and drop-in backup retained for rollback.

## Result

- `systemctl is-active` → active; `/healthz` → `{"version":"1.3.3"}`.
- HTTP MCP doctor → READY, **240 tools**.
- Lazy boot verified: `terminal_session_list` started Nucleus and answered.

## Gotcha worth remembering

After the rebuild, the runtime advertised only 209 tools and refused `terminal_session_list` and `keyword_extraction` as unknown. Cause: the runtime trusts a cell manifest only when its build digest matches the catalog, and cells rebuilt on this host hash differently from the catalog produced on lappy — two manifests were rejected and those cells vanished from the surface silently.

Fix: regenerate the catalog on the host that runs the cells (`node scripts/generate-tool-catalog.mjs --profile dev-workspace`), then restart. The runtime is on-demand, so nothing else changed. A profile-scoped catalog is a deployment artifact here; the repository copy is untouched.

## Rollback

```sh
sudo cp /etc/systemd/system/hela-runtime.service.d/10-nix-package.conf.bak-<stamp> \
        /etc/systemd/system/hela-runtime.service.d/10-nix-package.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart hela-runtime
```

The previous wrapper (`servy-update-20261114T063237Z`) and its Nix runtime are still on disk.

## 1.9.24 rollout (servy, 2026-11-19T21:01Z)

Second pass on the same day, carrying the RPC and search releases.

1. Checkouts pulled fast-forward: `project-mcp` b720edf (3.0.5), `terminal-mcp` 0088f0b (3.0.6), `researcher-mcp` eb257b8 (4.0.6), `browser-mcp` 8f0b39f (3.2.6), `hela-runtime` c2b02ff (1.3.6), ecosystem d193cc4 (1.9.24). The repository catalog copy was reverted before the pull — on this host it is a deployment artifact, as noted below.
2. Those four cells rebuilt (`npm run build`).
3. Catalog regenerated **on servy** with `--profile dev-workspace` before any restart, so the digests match the builds on this host.
4. Runtime packaged with Nix: `hela-runtime-1.3.6` at `/nix/store/g1npgvsii07mpclxzsxc9lm3gd15n12m-hela-runtime-1.3.6`, GC-rooted by `runtime-nix` inside the new deployment directory.
5. Staged wrapper at `~/.local/state/hela/deployments/servy-1.9.24-20261118T210125Z/runtime/bin/hela-runtime`, drop-in backed up to `10-nix-package.conf.bak-20261118T210124Z`, ExecStart switched, `daemon-reload`, restart.
6. Verified over HTTP: `/healthz` → `1.3.6`; `tools/list` → **239 tools** on the 8-cell `dev-workspace` profile (297 unique cell tools at profile all, minus Receptor 46 and Plastid 15, plus the 3 runtime tools); `hela.agent.run` present and the cell-local `agent_run` gone; `execute_command` with `cd /tmp && echo marker-ok` returned `stdout "marker-ok\n"`, exit 0; the scatter query returned zero Wikipedia hits.

239 rather than the earlier 240 because Mitosis now contributes one schema variant (24 tools) instead of the union across its four variants (29). Not a missing cell: Nucleus and Enzyme were both present and callable, which is the failure mode this host hit at 1.9.19.

Rollback is unchanged: restore the drop-in backup and restart. The 1.9.21 deployment directory and its Nix runtime stay on disk.

# Documentation refresh — 2026-11-06

Ecosystem **1.5.1** is a documentation-only source snapshot. The ten MCP cells remain **3.0.0**; runtime remains **1.2.0** at its existing implementation revision. [Current versions](current-versions.md) and [profile counts](generated-profile-counts.md) are generated from canonical metadata.

## Scope

- Audited all 12 repositories. Updated the ten cells' README version banners and generated canonical tool references; the runtime's existing 1.2.0 reference was already current.
- Completed all 16 English/Indonesian website pages, including current architecture, profiles, requirements, runtime behavior, diagnostics, privacy, and historical showcase labels.
- Corrected Codex keys and actual repository paths, including Plastid's `brain` entrypoint. Browser previews intentionally omit private environment values and are not byte-identical installation files.
- Regenerated seven committed client examples with a sanitized environment. The older seven-cell Compose file is explicitly a deployment scaffold, not full-profile or transport acceptance evidence.
- Preserved v1.0.0–v1.5.0 snapshots, historical release evidence, and independently versioned Blender/HyperFrames/vendor material.

## Verification

- Documentation generation is idempotent; `docs:check` and all **74** documentation/configuration regressions pass. These checks include local web links/anchors, unique IDs, JSON-LD, current versions, canonical tool lists, script ordering, and release cache-busting.
- CLI matrix: **80/80** profile/backend cases. Probe and inventory regressions: **4/4** each. Strict package/MCP/inventory/snapshot versions and revision pins: **11/11**.
- Standalone integration and safe cross-cell checks: **15/15** across ten servers, with no tool-name collisions in the feature-disabled probe environment.
- All eight profiles: **16/16** namespace-mode checks pass, with exact schemas, zero discovery startups, and safe read-only routing.
- Fresh native ARM probes validate all eight `dev-workspace` cells against the new documentation revisions. Schema parity retains both verified Nucleus build digests; compiled implementation bytes were reused, not rebuilt as a new software release.
- Browser checks: **64** visible configurator selections per language; **16** pages at **1200 px** and **390 px** widths without document-level horizontal overflow. Desktop/mobile screenshots were inspected. Canonical search links, successful copy, and denied-clipboard feedback were checked; failed clipboard writes no longer claim success.
- Current Markdown file-link scan: **104** references checked, no missing targets. This is not an exhaustive external-link availability guarantee.
- Secret scanning found only the pre-existing probe-test sentinel; no new credentials were added. Hardware, providers, and authenticated ACP/GUI sessions were not exercised by this documentation refresh.

## Publication boundaries

Plastid and Receptor had unrelated remote dependency updates. Documentation-only commits were merged into their default branches without discarding those updates. Snapshot v1.5.1 deliberately pins the documentation-only parents, not unvalidated dependency changes.

The Pages workflow validates generated documentation and its tests before publishing. Source commit: `7f95832b4f0b9e6ba3057ffbb7df84b62e2bcd91`. Published Pages commit: `3077d3f8d02436637b4322407c58621069dfe922`.

- [Ecosystem CI](https://github.com/Hela-Ecosystem/hela-mcp-ecosystem/actions/runs/42233639731): successful.
- [Validated site build/sync](https://github.com/Hela-Ecosystem/hela-mcp-ecosystem/actions/runs/42233639734): successful.
- [GitHub Pages deployment](https://github.com/Hela-Ecosystem/hela-mcp-ecosystem/actions/runs/42233666134): successful.
